 "sourceFile":"Relationships between lower limb muscle characteristics and force-velocity profiles derived during sprinting and jumping.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text ('Relationships between Lower Limb Muscle Characteristics and Force-Velocity Profiles Derived during Sprinting and Jumping') matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Study of 19 subelite male rugby league players. Vertical (squat jump) and horizontal (30 m sprint) force-velocity-power profiles were derived, and muscle fascicle length, pennation angle, thickness, volume and estimated fibre type (carnosine MRS) were measured with ultrasound, MRI and spectroscopy. Muscle fibre typology and muscle volume explained much of the variation in jump and sprint power and velocity variables (adjusted r2 up to about 0.63), with gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology and vastus lateralis volume the most frequent predictors.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Nineteen subelite players, all male, and one time point. The findings are regression associations, not causal effects of muscle characteristics on power. Fibre type was estimated indirectly from carnosine content, not biopsied.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the fibre-type findings as a basis for selecting players or designing training from a muscle test; the study explains variation in performance measures in a small subelite sample and does not test any training intervention.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Bellinger P, Bourne MN, Duhig S, Lievens E, Kennedy B, Martin A, et al. Relationships between Lower Limb Muscle Characteristics and Force-Velocity Profiles Derived during Sprinting and Jumping. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(7):1400-1411.",
   "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000002605",
   "abstract":"In 19 subelite male rugby league players, muscle fibre typology and muscle volume explained much of the variation in maximal power, force and velocity derived from jumping and sprinting force-velocity profiles.",
   "tldr":"Muscle fibre type and the size of key thigh and calf muscles were strongly associated with maximal power in jumping and sprinting in these players. This is a cross-sectional association, not a training result.",
   "methods":"Nineteen subelite male rugby league players performed squat jumps and 30 m sprints to derive vertical and horizontal force-velocity-power profiles. Fascicle length, pennation angle and thickness were measured with B-mode ultrasound, muscle volumes with MRI, and gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology with proton MR spectroscopy (carnosine). Stepwise regression was used to explain variation in profile variables.",
   "findings":"Variation in vertical maximal power was best explained by gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology and vastus lateralis volume (adjusted r2 = 0.440, p = 0.006). Variation in horizontal maximal power was best explained by adductor and vastus medialis volume and gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology (adjusted r2 = 0.634, p = 0.032). Velocity variables were best explained by gastrocnemius medialis fibre typology (adjusted r2 = 0.580 to 0.590, p < 0.001).",
   "limitations":"Small sample of 19 subelite male players. Cross-sectional, so associations cannot show causation. Fibre typology was estimated from carnosine MRS rather than measured directly.",
   "practicalImplications":"Muscle volume and estimated fibre type are associated with jump and sprint power and could be considered when profiling power in rugby players. Their value for guiding training change has not been tested here.",
   "athleteDev":"Muscle volume and estimated fibre type explained much of the variation in jump and sprint power in these players, which supports measuring muscle characteristics when profiling power, though not as a direct training prescription.",
   "rtp":"This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It was done in healthy subelite players and does not test whether muscle characteristics or force-velocity profiles indicate readiness to return after injury."
 }
}

 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Research & Analytics","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Laboratory study in which helmeted crash test dummies were propelled into each other in seven helmet-to-helmet configurations representing on-field American football impacts. Helmet and head kinematics were measured with instrumentation and optical motion capture. The helmet translated 12 to 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees relative to the head, and its peak linear acceleration was about 2 to 5 times that of the head.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample is crash test dummies, not athletes, and only seven impact configurations were tested. The findings describe helmet and head motion in these configurations and do not show injury risk for players.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the helmet-head motion results as a direct measure of how much a helmet protects a player; the study shows helmet motion relative to a dummy head in set impacts, and its main message is about measurement method.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Joodaki H, Bailey A, Lessley D, Funk J, et al. Relative Motion between the Helmet and Head in Football Impact Test. J Biomech Eng. 2019.",
   "doi":"10.1115/1.4043038",
   "abstract":"Seven helmet-to-helmet impact configurations were simulated with helmeted crash test dummies. Helmets translated 12 to 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees with respect to the head, and helmet peak linear acceleration was 2 to 5 times the head's. The authors conclude that head motion must be measured independently of the helmet.",
   "tldr":"Helmets move noticeably relative to the head during football impacts, so video tracking of the helmet alone does not capture head biomechanics. Head motion needs its own measurement.",
   "methods":"Laboratory impact experiment. Seven helmet-to-helmet configurations were simulated by propelling helmeted crash test dummies into each other. Helmet and head kinematics were measured with instrumentation and an optical motion capture system, analysed from 10 ms before contact to 20 ms after loss of contact.",
   "findings":"Helmets translated 12 to 41 mm and rotated up to 37 degrees relative to the head. Peak resultant linear acceleration of the helmet was about 2 to 5 times that of the head. Peak resultant angular velocity of the helmet ranged from 37 percent less to 71 percent more than the head, depending on the impact condition.",
   "limitations":"Crash test dummies rather than human heads or players. Seven impact configurations only. The findings are specific to the test set-up and the dummy's head and neck.",
   "practicalImplications":"Helmet-mounted sensors or video of helmets are not enough to estimate head motion in football impacts. Head-mounted or independent head measurement should be used where head kinematics are needed.",
   "athleteDev":"Staff using helmet video or helmet-based impact data to estimate head motion should treat it as a measure of helmet movement, not the head, which matters for how impact data are interpreted across football practice and games.",
   "rtp":"This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It uses crash test dummies and cannot be used to judge whether an injured player is ready to return."
 }
}
